title: Big dataset — glove-100-angular (cosine, 1.2M)
subtitle: MyVector · vsql_vector · pgvector — 1.18M × 100-d word embeddings, cosine, published ground truth
nav: ← cross-engine (fashion-mnist) · MySQL versions · real-dataset · village
description: The big-dataset round: glove-100-angular — 1.18 million 100-d GloVe word embeddings with a cosine metric (vs the 60k×784 L2 fashion-mnist on the other pages). Recall@10 is scored against the dataset's published exact neighbors. GloVe is a genuinely hard ANN benchmark, so recall sits well below the ~0.99 of fashion-mnist — the interesting comparison is the recall/throughput tradeoff each engine strikes at this scale. Full metrics via MyVector's harness.
caveats: ⚡ MyVector here is current main (PR #278 + #280), re-measured on glove 2026-11-10: the current-main build (NEON cosine kernel + keepPrunedConnections, plus #280 which removed the ANN-rewrite overhead), engine-isolated on A2 like the other engines. PR #280 lifts glove QPS +35–48% across the sweep (e.g. ef=50 601→872, ef=200 287→424) at unchanged recall, on top of #278. pgvector and vsql are unaffected by #280 and keep their engine-isolated numbers, so MyVector’s matched-recall lead here widens (e.g. ~872 QPS vs pgvector ~281 / vsql ~360 at recall ~0.73). (Both are merged to main.)

Dataset: glove-100-angular (ann-benchmarks) — 1.18M train × 100-d GloVe word vectors, 10k test, cosine. HNSW M=16, ef_construction=200. Recall is intrinsically lower than on fashion-mnist — GloVe is a hard, high-overlap embedding space.

Reading the sweep: MyVector tunes for throughput, so it reaches each recall at a lower ef_search — its per-point dots sit lower-and-righter, but at matched recall (the table above) it serves the most QPS across the mid-to-high recall range. This re-measured optimized run sweeps ef=10→800 (the prior scalar run also went to ef=1600/3200, reaching recall 0.985, confirming MyVector doesn't plateau — the optimized build would reach those recalls even faster).

Engine-isolated: each engine was benchmarked with the other engines stopped, so its 1.2M index build had the full A2 host (24 GB) to itself — building four 1.2M HNSW indexes with all servers resident OOMs the box. pgvector also needed --shm-size=4g for its parallel build.

Full metrics via MyVector's harness: build, insert QPS, exact brute-force KNN (QPS + p50/p99), ANN (QPS + p50/p99), recall@10 vs published ground truth. Headline cards are the warm ef_search=200 point.

Build time — super-linear, not a threading gap (verified): the same 1.2M HNSW index build took MyVector ~46 min and pgvector ~33 min but vsql_vector ~7 hours (the index build specifically; vsql's insert was ~3 min). We checked whether vsql was single-threaded — it isn't: its build runs ~4 threads (measured ~410% CPU, matching innodb_ddl_threads=4). The real cause is that vsql's build scales super-linearly: a 40k-row build takes ~100 s, but 1.18M took ~7 h — ~256× the time for ~30× the rows (≈ O(N^1.6)), far beyond the ~1 h a near-linear extrapolation predicts. So its graph construction degrades at scale (likely memory/cache-bound) while MyVector's and pgvector's stay efficient at 1.2M. Each engine used its default build path on the same 8-core host. MariaDB is excluded (re-confirmed 2026-11-06, quantified): a fresh MHNSW build on glove-100 (1.18M) — with a generous 4 GB InnoDB pool + 2 GB mhnsw_max_cache_size, so not a cache-thrashing artifact — did not complete within a 4 h hard cap (reached ~819k/1.18M, ~69%), and a second attempt with a 10 h cap also did not complete. Its online insert/build rate decays as the graph grows (311k rows at 36 min → 529k at 1.6 h → 819k at 3.6 h on the first run; ~500k at 1.5 h on the second), so the full 1.18M build needs >10 h — impractical at this scale. So MariaDB is genuinely unable to build the 1.2M cosine index in a usable window; it appears on the 60k×784 fashion-mnist pages where its build does complete.
Hardware: Ampere A2 host (8 vCPU / 24 GB), one engine resident at a time.
